issues.issue: The sentence is garbled ("the ‘Tru is offering shares. beneficial interest") so the identity of the offeror and the thing offered is not cleanly stated. The defect is transcription-level rather than substantive, and the sense is recoverable.

This offers Shares to "qualified institutional purchasers," while the cover legend furnishes the Memorandum to "qualified institutional or accredited investors," and the 1940 Act section relies on Section 3(c)(1) rather than 3(c)(7). The mismatch in investor class descriptions is a minor internal inconsistency.

"[C]ontinuous source of managed investment for cash collateral" states a purpose in terms (continuity, cash-collateral suitability) that carry no defined boundary. A court could be asked what standard of liquidity that purpose imports.

The stated cash-collateral purpose sits uneasily with the operative Investment Policies permitting five-year maturities ("(d) Maturity of Portfolio Instruments") and 15% illiquid securities. A purpose-versus-operative-term argument is available.

"[C]onsideration specified by Wells Fargo from time to time" must be read with the fixed $10.00 initial offering price and the daily "then applicable value per Share" in Terms of the Offering. The relationship is workable but not spelled out.

Wells Fargo acting as both trustee and self-appointed investment manager must be read against the "Conflicts of Interest" section and the "Limitations of Liability" carve-out for duties "to the Trust." No direct contradiction appears.

"Wells Fargo" is defined as Wells Fargo Bank Minnesota, N.A., yet Galliard is described as a wholly owned subsidiary of that defined entity rather than of Wells Fargo & Company named in "The Trustee." The defined-term usage is loose.

"[S]ole discretion" over how much of the Fund Galliard advises is unbounded and gives no standard against which the allocation could be measured. Whether an implied good-faith limit applies is arguable.

An "undivided proportionate interest in all assets and liabilities of the Fund" sits against the statement that ownership gives Shareholders no "title in or to the property of the Trust." The two can be harmonised as economic versus legal interest, but the tension is visible.

"[R]elatively stable value per Share" is vague: it gives no tolerance band and no benchmark, and it is immediately disclaimed in the same sentence. What Wells Fargo promised to "seek" is exactly the kind of phrase parties read differently.

This stability undertaking must be squared with "Valuation of the Trust," which requires assets to be valued each Business Day at "then current market value." A stable per-Share value and daily market valuation pull in different directions.

The sentence breaks off at "the then applicable value per Share (as", leaving the cross-reference to the valuation definition incomplete. The referent is inferable from the "Valuation of the Trust" heading that follows.

The text is scrambled ("The minimum required investment for the securities lending program, Initial purchases will be determined by Wells Fargo In the efficient management of"), so as written no minimum and no standard can be identified. "Efficient management" also supplies no measurable criterion.

"[T]hen current market value" is undefined and gives no method for securities without an active market, which the Fund is expressly permitted to hold under the 15% illiquid-securities limit. The valuation basis is exactly what a court would be asked to fix.

Daily market-value valuation is difficult to reconcile with the undertakings to maintain a "relatively stable value per Share" and a "stable $10.00 price per Share" in Terms of the Offering and Investment Objectives. The instrument never says which controls the redemption price.

Wells Fargo is said to perform accounting services, while "Expenses" states that certain accounting services will be provided by Forum Accounting Services under a separate contract. The division of accounting responsibility is left unclear.
The subject is garbled ("The ives will declare a dividend"), so the provision does not say who declares the dividend. The sense (the Fund or Wells Fargo) is recoverable from context.

"[A]ll expenses Incurred In connection with the acquisition, ownership and transfer of Its investments" is a general phrase followed by an "including" list, leaving the catch-all's reach against the enumerated items open. Whether unlisted charges fall inside the general words is the classic ejusdem generis question.

This expense-bearing clause must be read with "Neither Wells Fargo nor any of its affiliates ... will receive any fees or compensation from the Trust," and with the Forum fee payable on average daily net assets. Which of the three governs an accounting charge is not stated.

"[A]ny fees or compensation from the Trust" is narrow in a way that leaves open compensation received elsewhere, for example out of securities-lending revenue split with lenders. The scope of the no-fee promise is the arguable point.

The flat no-compensation statement sits against the immediately following paragraph under which Forum is paid a fee based on the Fund's average daily net assets pursuant to a contract entered into by Wells Fargo. Who bears that fee is not reconciled.

The provider is named "Forum Accounting Services, LLC" in the first sentence and "Forum Financial" in the second, and the payer of the fee is never identified. The mismatch of names and the missing payer are both on the face of the clause.

A fee "based on ... the average daily net assets of the Fund" implies a Fund-borne charge not listed among the expenses the Fund bears in "Expenses," while Wells Fargo is said to have entered the contract. The two paragraphs do not settle incidence of the fee.

Using affiliated brokers must be read with the "Conflicts of Interest" section and the no-affiliate-compensation statement in "Expenses." Brokerage paid to affiliates arguably is compensation flowing from Fund assets.

The flat prohibition on transfer or assignment sits against "Tax Matters," which says Wells Fargo merely "intends to restrict transfers of ownership" to avoid publicly-traded-partnership status. If transfers are already barred outright the tax provision is redundant, suggesting the bar is not absolute.

The seven-day cash payment obligation is subject to a right to postpone payment or suspend redemptions "In certain circumstances as specified in the Declaration of Trust," a circumstance set unbounded on the face of this document. Whether the exception swallows the rule is precisely what parties would fight over.

The postponement/suspension right must be reconciled with the preceding sentence giving Shareholders the right to require redemption "no less often than as of the close of each Business Day" and with the Fund's daily-liquidity objective in Investment Objectives. The document never states which prevails.

The exculpation is drafted as a blanket "no liability" subject to a proviso listing "bad faith, willful misconduct, negligence or reckless disregard," so including ordinary negligence leaves the clause's protective scope genuinely unclear. The standard of care actually preserved is the arguable point.

The cover legend states that "no legal liability is assumed or is to be implied against" Wells Fargo or its agents with respect to the Memorandum, an unqualified disclaimer, whereas this clause expressly preserves liability for negligence. The two liability statements are not aligned.

Rights are said to be only those "provided In the Declaration of Trust," which the Memorandum elsewhere says may be amended by the Trustee at any time without Shareholder approval. Read together, the Shareholder's rights are defeasible in a way this clause does not disclose.

Limited liability "under the terms of the Declaration of Trust" is qualified by the same document's classification of the Trust and Fund as partnerships for tax purposes and by the amendment power in "Amendment of Declaration of Trust." No direct contradiction, but the source of the protection is external.

The denial of any "title in or to the property of the Trust" sits against the statement in Terms of the Offering that each Share "represents an undivided proportionate interest in all assets and liabilities of the Fund." The two characterisations of the Shareholder's interest differ.

Indemnification "from the assets of the Trust" for Shareholders held personally liable overlaps with the Trust's indemnity of Wells Fargo and agents in the same section, both payable from the same assets. Priority between the two indemnities is unaddressed.

The closing qualifier "unless expressly required under the Maryland Act" is grammatically detached, so it is unclear whether it qualifies the amendment power, the absence of Shareholder approval, or the notice. The stated premise ("Because the Declaration does not confer any independent rights") is also assertion rather than definition.

An unlimited unilateral amendment power is hard to square with provisions that fix Shareholder entitlements by reference to the Declaration of Trust, such as "Shares will be deemed to be personal property, giving only the rights provided In the Declaration of Trust" and the redemption right. Those rights could be amended away.

"[T]he obligations of Wells Fargo to the Trust are not exclusive" must be read against the exculpation clause's reference to Wells Fargo's "duties to the Trust" and its role as sole trustee and self-appointed investment manager. How far this disclaimer cuts down trustee duties is arguable.

"[M]ade Independently from those other accounts" is a factual assurance with no defined content or procedure, so what independence requires cannot be measured. The word carries more than one plausible reading.
The sentence is transposed ("Wells Fa continue In that capacity ... rgo and wil"), leaving the retention/removal statement scrambled. The intended sense is recoverable.

The text is transposed around the commencement date ("commence 0 erations on July 2 | has no performance history"), though the date and the no-history statement survive. Nothing substantive turns on the garble.

"[H]igh-quality," "safety of principal" and "daily liquidity requirements" are each undefined and set no measurable boundary, and "prime considerations" does not say what yields to what. These are the words a disappointed investor and the manager would read differently.

The safety-of-principal and daily-liquidity objective is in tension with the operative guidelines permitting five-year maximum maturities, 15% illiquid securities and asset-backed and mortgage-backed holdings. Whether the objective constrains the guidelines or merely aspires is unresolved.

"[E]ndeavor to maintain a stable $10.00 price per Share" is an undertaking of effort with no standard, immediately negated by a no-assurance disclaimer in the same sentence. Whether it is a promise at all is arguable.

A stable $10.00 per-Share price cannot easily be squared with "Valuation of the Trust," which requires daily valuation at "then current market value," and with the redemption price being "the valuation per Share as determined by Wells Fargo." The pricing basis is left inconsistent.

The clause first says the Trust "may only invest in ... obligations rated in the highest short-term rating category by one of two" NRSROs, then permits obligations rated by "at least one" NRSRO and, in (ii), obligations that are "unrated" altogether. "[O]nly ... rated" against "are unrated" is a contradiction on the face of the provision.

A highest-short-term-rating-only quality test is hard to reconcile with the permitted-investment list in (b), which includes mortgage-backed, asset-backed and corporate notes, bonds and debentures that carry long-term rather than short-term ratings. The two subsections do not fit together.

The bulleted categories are broad and undefined — "Commercial paper and participations," "Asset-backed securities," "Corporate notes, bonds, debentures" — and the clause does not say whether the list is exhaustive or whether structured instruments fall within any bullet. Which side of the list a given instrument falls on is exactly the construction question.

The list is headed "Portfolio Diversification" yet imposes no diversification requirement, and it authorises long-dated categories that sit against the "(a) Portfolio Quality" highest-short-term-rating limit and the safety/daily-liquidity objective. The permitted categories and the quality gate are not harmonised.
"[O]bligations of any one issuer" is undefined for structured vehicles and conduits, where the issuer, sponsor and guarantor may differ. The concentration test's unit of measurement is not fixed.

The limit runs on "the Fund," whereas the adjacent Portfolio Quality and Portfolio Maturity guidelines are framed as limits on "the Trust." The Trust/Fund shift makes the level at which each limit bites uncertain.

"[V]ariable rate securities" is undefined, and the guidelines elsewhere treat variable, floating and variable rate demand obligations as distinct categories. Which instruments count toward the 35% cap is arguable.

The Investment Restrictions section refers to "variable rate obligations" and the maturity rules to "variable and floating rate obligations," without saying whether the 35% cap covers floating rate instruments too. The categories are not aligned across the guidelines.

The 15% illiquid cap defined by Rule 2a-7 sits against the next sentence, which deems Rule 144A private placements "generally ... liquid" on a test that reads backwards. Whether 144A paper counts toward the 15% cap is left unresolved.

The sentence is inverted: private placements are said to be "considered liquid unless at least two broker/dealers provide an active secondary market," which makes dealer support a reason for illiquidity. As written the test produces the opposite of its evident intent.
Because of the inversion, the provision undercuts the immediately preceding 15% illiquid-securities cap measured by SEC Rule 2a-7. The two sentences cannot both be applied as written.

"[A]ssets scheduled to mature overnight" is not tied to a measurement date or to the deeming rules used elsewhere for maturity, so whether reset dates and demand features count is open. The 20% floor is otherwise clear.

The 90-day cap is imposed on "the Trust's portfolio," while other limits in the same guidelines run on "the Fund"; the Trust is a multi-series vehicle of which the Fund is one series. Whether the cap is measured Fund-by-Fund or across the Trust is unstated.

The enumeration is misnumbered, with two clauses labelled "(ii)", and the "shortest of the following" rule is stated without saying what happens when an obligation has none of the three features. The numbering error is on the face of the text.

The "shortest of" rule here is immediately qualified by the "longer of" rule for variable rate demand obligations in the next sentence and by the "shorter of" rule in "(d) Maturity of Portfolio Instruments." Three different deeming rules for overlapping instrument types sit in adjacent paragraphs.

"[V]ariable rate demand obligation" is undefined and overlaps with the "variable rate obligations" and "obligations with put features" referred to in the surrounding sentences. Which instruments attract the longer-of rule is the arguable point.

This "longer of" rule directly reverses the "shortest of" rule in the preceding sentence and the "shorter of" rule in "(d) Maturity of Portfolio Instruments" for what may be the same instrument. The instrument never states which subsection governs a given security.

"[M]aximum maturity of a security" is not tied to a definition — legal final, expected average life or reset date — even though the surrounding paragraphs supply competing deeming rules. For amortising asset-backed paper the applicable measure is genuinely contestable.

A five-year maximum maturity is difficult to reconcile with the objective of "safety of principal and daily liquidity requirements" and with the 90-day maximum dollar-weighted average maturity in "(c) Portfolio Maturity." Whether five-year paper was ever contemplated for cash collateral is exactly the whole-instrument question.

This "shorter of" deeming rule for variable and floating rate obligations contradicts the "longer of" rule for variable rate demand obligations in "(c) Portfolio Maturity." The same instrument can fall within both descriptions and receive two different maturities.
A one-year repo maturity must be read with the 90-day dollar-weighted average maturity limit and the 20% overnight requirement. The limits are compatible, but the interaction is not stated.

Using the repo end date rather than the underlying obligation's maturity must be read with the issuer-concentration exception for "repurchase agreements collateralized by" Government obligations, which looks through to the collateral. The two rules treat repos inconsistently.

The operative sentence is broken — "the Investment determines is In the best Interests of the Trust" — so the provision never states what the Investment Manager must do on a downgrade. As written it imposes no ascertainable obligation.

The clause turns on "the Requisite NRSROs" and "an Unrated Security," capitalised terms that appear nowhere else; "(a) Portfolio Quality" defines only "NRSRO" and uses "at least one" rating agency. The downgrade trigger cannot be matched to the quality test.

"[T]o the extent permitted by law (i.e., ...)" uses "i.e." to introduce what reads like an illustration, so it is unclear whether the parenthesis exhaustively defines the permitted vehicles or merely exemplifies them. The general-versus-specific reach of the parenthetical is the issue.

Investment company securities appear nowhere in the "(b) Portfolio Diversification" list of authorised investments, and fund shares are not rated obligations meeting "(a) Portfolio Quality." This permission sits outside both guidelines.

"[A] leading money market index such as Fed Funds or LIBOR" pairs an undefined general standard with two named examples, leaving open whether indices like CMT, prime or COFI qualify. That is a straightforward ejusdem generis problem.
"Dual index" and "inverse floaters" are technical terms left undefined, and structured instruments can be argued in or out of them. The prohibition's edge is not fixed.

The statement that Share value "will change with the change in value of the Trust's investments" is difficult to square with the undertakings to maintain a "stable $10.00 price per Share" and a "relatively stable value per Share." The disclosure and the pricing undertaking point in different directions.

The risk factor refers to "the counterparty to a derivative," but derivatives appear nowhere in the "(b) Portfolio Diversification" list of authorised investments. Whether derivatives were permitted is left inconsistent between the two sections.

The reference to duration extension in asset-backed and mortgage-backed securities sits against the 90-day dollar-weighted average maturity cap and the daily liquidity objective. The disclosure implies exposures the guidelines appear to limit.

Acknowledged illiquidity risk sits against the daily-redemption right and seven-day cash payment obligation in "Transferability of Shares and Redemption Rights." The document does not say how illiquidity affects that redemption promise.

"[A] limited number of investors" is not tied to the 100-person ceiling relied on in the Section 3(c)(1) paragraph, and Rule 506 permits a different count. The two eligibility limits are stated independently.

The clause exempts the Fund from "the registration requirements of the 1946 Act," a statute that does not exist; the heading and the next sentence refer to the 1940 Act. The misstatement is plainly a typographical slip.

Reliance on Section 3(c)(1)'s 100-beneficial-owner ceiling sits against the Summary's offering to "qualified institutional purchasers" and the cover legend's "qualified institutional or accredited investors," which point toward a different exemption. The eligibility framework is not internally aligned.
The sentence is cut off ("on an ongoing basl") and "appropriate representations and undertakings" supplies no content or standard. What the purchaser must give is undefined.
The passage breaks off mid-sentence ("the rules and regulations of the United States Department of") so the ERISA reference is incomplete. It is advisory in nature and imposes no obligation.

Partnership classification for federal tax sits against the Summary's characterisation of the vehicle as a Maryland business trust whose Shareholders enjoy corporate-style limited liability. The characterisations are reconcilable but stated without linkage.

An intention to "restrict transfers of ownership" presupposes that transfers are possible, whereas "Transferability of Shares and Redemption Rights" states flatly that Shares "may not be transferred or assigned." The two provisions describe different transfer regimes.

Allocation of income and deduction "as determined according to the Declaration of Trust" leaves the mechanics outside this instrument, alongside the Trustee's unilateral power to amend that Declaration. The allocation basis is therefore not fixed by the Memorandum.
"[W]ill be passed on by KPMG LLP" does not say whether an opinion will be delivered, to whom, or on what. The undertaking's content is indeterminate.

KPMG is elsewhere identified as the Trust's independent auditor serving "at the sole discretion of Wells Fargo," so tax opinion work is assigned to the same firm. The relationship between the two roles is unaddressed.
"[S]hould be exempt" and "should not cause" are hedged predictions rather than statements of entitlement, and "absent any other nexus to Maryland" is undefined. What was represented is arguable.

Describing the Memorandum as "an overview" fits the cover legend's statement that the summary "does not purport to be a complete summary" and is qualified by the Declaration of Trust. No conflict emerges, though it weakens reliance on the operative-sounding guidelines.

"[A]ny other materials available to Wells Fargo relating to the Trust" is an unbounded catch-all following the specific reference to the Declaration of Trust. What an investor was entitled to see is left open.

The invitation to review any available materials sits against the cover legend's statement that no person is authorised to give information other than as contained in the Memorandum or the supplemental data. The two describe different information regimes.
"[T]he divulgence of any of its contents" is absolute and unqualified, with no carve-out for advisers or legally compelled disclosure. Its practical boundary would have to be construed.

The blanket ban on divulging contents sits against "ERISA Considerations" and "Tax Matters," which direct investors to review the offering with their legal and tax advisers. The instrument both forbids and contemplates disclosure to third parties.

"By accepting this offering memorandum, the recipient agrees" purports to bind by receipt, and the return trigger "upon delivery of updated offering materials" is not tied to any obligation to deliver such materials. Whether a binding obligation arises and when it is triggered are both open.
